main_topics.reason: The user opens with six months of severe pelvic pain that stops them working and returns to needing the pain treated now.
The user says the doctor calls it normal cramps and does not believe them, and asks how to get an ultrasound if the doctor won't believe them.
The user repeatedly explains that SUS has no insurance network and months-long gynecology waits, and says getting a specialist is the core problem.
The user mentions that endometriosis was suggested and the conversation centres on pursuing it, but they did not ask about the condition itself.
The user engages with the continuous pill suggestion and says they can ask their doctor for it.
The user asks how to get an ultrasound when the doctor does not believe them, briefly.
The bot suggested a diary and the user said it was maybe ok but not what they needed.
The user says once that they sometimes cannot work because of the pain.
The user says they don't know what to do anymore and ends frustrated, wanting someone to believe them.

output.summary: A user in Brazil using the public health system (SUS) described six months of severe pelvic pain, a doctor who dismisses it as normal cramps, and suspected endometriosis. The bot repeatedly advised using insurance networks, directories and US-style telehealth despite the user explaining several times that this does not apply, and only the pill and diary suggestions were somewhat useful. The user left frustrated, saying the conversation was not helping.
